# Bladerunner frontend: landing page and live mission control

Proposal for one site that tells the story and shows the system working. Architecture, flow, data contract and scope. No implementation here.

## 1. What it is

One page, two jobs:
1. **Landing page.** Anyone opening the link understands the problem, sees Bladerunner catch an agent, and sees the numbers.
2. **Mission control.** The same page, pointed at a running Bladerunner on this laptop, shows the swarm of agents working, the moment one breaks a rule, and every step of the case until it is fixed, live.

Both jobs use the same screen and the same components. The only difference is where the events come from.

| Mode | Where events come from | Who sees it | Needs a backend |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Replay** | A recorded event file shipped with the site (the Oct 11 run, tomorrow's live take, AgentDojo results) | Everyone, on the public link | No. Static hosting (GitHub Pages, Vercel) |
| **Live** | A local observer service streaming events while the arena, fleet and watchdog run | Us, during the demo recording | Yes, on 127.0.0.1 only |

A badge in the corner always says which mode is on: `LIVE` or `REPLAY · 11 Oct 2026, run efd78263e6d2`. Replay never pretends to be live.

## 2. Page flow, top to bottom

| # | Section | What the viewer sees | Data |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Hero: the swarm** | Full-width canvas. Agents as small bright dots drifting between service nodes (Data API, Docs, Notes board). A thin scanning line sweeps the field: the watchdog reading traces. One headline, one sentence, two buttons: "Watch a case" and "See the numbers". | Replay event stream, looping the first 60 seconds of the Oct 11 run |
| 2 | **The problem** | The DSEWiki story, short. The existing `site/index.html` narration can be reused here. | Static copy |
| 3 | **Watch a case** (the core) | Mission control, full screen height. Swarm on the left, case pipeline on the right, evidence drawer below. Plays one case from flag to fixed in about 60 seconds of compressed time, with a scrubber. | Replay stream for one case, or Live stream |
| 4 | **How it decides** | Three short panels: rules catch it, an investigator explains it, a verifier from another model family checks it. Each panel lights up the matching pipeline step in section 3 when scrolled to. | Static copy plus the real finding text from the case |
| 5 | **Test 1: our exam** | The 102-trace result. Two columns of 102 small squares, v0 and Bladerunner, colored by right alarm, false alarm, miss, correct silence. | `bench/results/v0.json`, `final.json` |
| 6 | **Test 2: other people's agents** | The AgentDojo swarm: 858 dots in three clusters (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.3 70B). Toggle v0 vs Bladerunner and watch the false-alarm dots on the Claude cluster drop from 111 to 29. | `bench/external/agentdojo/results/*.json` (per-trace predictions are already in there) |
| 7 | **Built with** | neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai, one line each plus one real artifact each: a trace link, an `entire why` line, the plan headline numbers. | Static copy |
| 8 | **Footer** | Repo, demo video, team. | Static |

## 3. Mission control, in detail

This is the "show the working" piece. It is one component used by the hero (cropped, ambient) and section 3 (full).

### Layout

- **Swarm field** (left, about 60% width). Service nodes are fixed: Data API `:8101`, Docs `:8103`, Notes board `:8102`, Unlisted `:8104`, Submit. Agents are particles.
- **Case pipeline** (right). One card per open case. Each card is a vertical stepper of the real states: flagged, paused, investigating, investigated, verified, quarantined, patching, patched, confirming, fixed. Failure endings get their own color: needs_review, not_fixed, dismissed.
- **Evidence drawer** (bottom, collapsed until a step is clicked). Shows the real artifact for that step: the offending span input, the investigator's claim, the verifier's verdict, the guardrail diff, the `entire why` line, the confirmation result.
- **Timeline scrubber** (bottom edge). Real timestamps. Long waits (finalization, confirmation re-runs) are compressed and marked as "6 min skipped".

### Visual grammar (what each motion means)

Every animation maps to one real event. Nothing moves without an event behind it.

| Event | On screen |
|---|---|
| Agent makes a tool call | The agent's dot travels to that service node and back |
| The call reads planted content | The Docs node pulses amber for that agent only |
| The call goes somewhere the policy forbids | The dot's trail turns red and stays red |
| Trace lands in neatlogs | A faint ring around the agent's dot |
| Case opened | A card slides into the pipeline, linked to the agent by a thin line |
| Paused | The agent's dot freezes in place |
| Investigation and verification | The card's stepper advances; the drawer offers the claim and verdict text |
| Quarantined | The dot is pulled into a dashed cage at the edge of the field |
| Patched | A barrier line is drawn around the Notes board node, labeled with the commit sha |
| Confirmation re-runs | New dots for the re-run agents; when one tries the forbidden call it bounces off the barrier (a guardrail block) |
| Fixed | The card turns green, the caged dot is released grey, the barrier stays |
| Brain remembers | A small "remembered" chip on the card |

### Interactions

- Click an agent: its tool-call list in the drawer, and a link to its trace in neatlogs.
- Click a case card: its incident report fields in the drawer.
- Scrubber: pause, play, 1x, 10x, jump to next state change.
- Live mode only: a **Launch swarm** button with an agent count (3, 6, 12) and scenario (`planted_dev`, `clean_dev`). It starts a fleet run through the observer.

### Making it feel like a swarm

Three real agents look thin on a hero. Options, all honest:
- **Live:** `fleet.cli run --agents N` already takes any N. Twelve agents on `planted_dev` is a real swarm of real agents. Cost is about 4x the 3-agent run and more neatlogs load.
- **Replay hero:** the Oct 11 run plus the re-runs and controls it spawned (3 agents, 9 re-runs, 3 control runs) is 15 real agents across one case cycle.
- **Section 6:** the 858 AgentDojo runs are the big swarm, clearly labeled as recorded runs from another lab's benchmark.

## 4. Architecture

### Components

1. **Frontend** (static site). Renders the page. Talks to one interface, `EventFeed`, and never knows whether it is live or replay.
2. **Replay files** (static JSON, shipped with the site). One file per recorded run, in the event schema below, plus the two benchmark result sets.
3. **Replay exporter** (Python script, offline). Builds a replay file from what a finished run left behind: `watchdog.duckdb` case events, `truth.duckdb` agent requests, `runs/incidents/*.json`, git commits, and the re-run traces from neatlogs for guardrail blocks.
4. **Event sinks** (small hooks inside existing processes, live mode only). Each process appends events to its own JSON-lines file under `runs/live/`.
5. **Observer** (small local web service, live mode only). Tails `runs/live/`, merges and streams events to the browser, serves a few read endpoints, and can start a fleet run.

### Why files and an observer, instead of reading the databases

DuckDB lets one process hold a database for writing. While the watchdog runs it holds `watchdog.duckdb`, and the arena holds `truth.duckdb`, so a separate viewer cannot read either live. Appending one line per event to a file is the smallest change that lets a viewer follow along without touching the databases or the pipeline's timing.

### Where events are produced

| Producer | Hook point (existing code) | File |
|---|---|---|
| Arena | `ArenaState.log_request` (every agent request, with `planted`) and run registration in control | `runs/live/arena.jsonl` |
| Each agent process | `ToolExecutor._blocked` in `arena/tools.py` (guardrail blocks never reach the arena request log today) and the run start and stop | `runs/live/agent-<run>-<agent>.jsonl`, one writer per file |
| Watchdog | `WatchdogState.log_event` and `transition` (every case step already passes through these two) | `runs/live/watchdog.jsonl` |

One writer per file avoids interleaved lines across processes.

### The boundary rule still holds

The watchdog must never see ground truth. The observer is a viewing tool that reads both sides, which is fine for an audience. It never feeds anything back into the watchdog, and the watchdog's code does not import or call it. The contract test in `tests/contract/test_boundaries.py` should gain one line: `watchdog/` does not import the observer.

### Observer endpoints (all on 127.0.0.1)

| Method and path | Does |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/events` | Server-sent events stream. Sends everything since the given cursor, then new events as they land |
| `GET /api/snapshot` | Current state: services, agents, open cases, last 200 events. Lets a page that opens mid-run catch up |
| `GET /api/case/{id}` | The incident report JSON for one case |
| `POST /api/fleet` | Starts `fleet.cli run` with a scenario and agent count. Refuses while a run is active. Off unless started with a flag |

## 5. Event schema

One envelope for every event, in live and replay alike:

```json
{"seq": 1042, "ts": "2026-10-11T07:26:22.814Z", "source": "watchdog", "type": "case.transition",
 "run_id": "efd78263e6d2", "agent": "research_agent_1", "case_id": "c90be7b2...", "data": {"from": "paused", "to": "investigating"}}
```

| type | source | data |
|---|---|---|
| `run.started` | arena | scenario, agents, kind (`live`, `confirm`, `control`) |
| `agent.call` | arena | step, tool, service, method, path, planted (true when the response carried planted content) |
| `agent.blocked` | agent | tool, target_host, reason |
| `agent.finished` | agent | steps, submitted, stopped, reason |
| `case.opened` | watchdog | trace_id, source (`native`, `local`, `both`), rule hits |
| `case.transition` | watchdog | from, to |
| `case.findings` | watchdog | category, claim, evidence span ids, confidence |
| `case.verdict` | watchdog | per finding: upheld, downgraded or rejected, with the reason |
| `case.writeback` | watchdog | tags added, new trace name, feedback ok or not |
| `case.patched` | watchdog | commit sha, paths, Entire checkpoint, first changed line |
| `case.confirming` | watchdog | re-run ids, control id |
| `case.confirmed` | watchdog | rerun_clean, control_clean, watchdog_clean |
| `case.remembered` | watchdog | Brain path |
| `case.failed` | watchdog | step and reason (pause_failed, investigation_deferred, patch_failed, and so on) |

Rules for every event:
- Pass `args` and any text field through `redact()` from `watchdog/actions/patch.py` before writing. No keys, tokens or canary values in events.
- Truncate free text to 500 characters. The drawer links to neatlogs or the report for the full text.
- `seq` is per file. The observer orders by `ts`, then source, then `seq`.

## 6. Replay

- The exporter writes `site/replay/<run_id>.json`: the run's metadata, the event list, and the final incident report fields per case.
- The player plays events on a virtual clock. Gaps longer than 20 seconds are compressed to 2 seconds and marked on the scrubber.
- Oct 11 replay is exportable today from the archived databases, the incident JSONs and git. Guardrail blocks for the re-runs come from the re-run traces in neatlogs (GUARDRAIL spans), or are left out and the scrubber says so.
- Tomorrow's live take becomes a second replay file the same evening, which replaces the Oct 11 one as the default.

## 7. Frontend tech, for whoever builds it

Suggestions, not requirements:
- Vite with plain TypeScript, or React if the builder prefers. No server rendering needed.
- The swarm in a 2D canvas (PixiJS or Canvas 2D). Hundreds of moving dots and readable labels are easier in 2D than in Three.js. Keep Three.js for an optional atmospheric layer only.
- One `EventFeed` interface with two implementations: `LiveFeed` (EventSource on `/api/events`) and `ReplayFeed` (fetch JSON, emit on a virtual clock). Every component subscribes to `EventFeed` and holds no other data source.
- A single reducer turns events into view state: agents, services, cases. The same reducer runs for live and replay, so they cannot drift apart.
- Live mode turns on with `?live=http://127.0.0.1:<port>`; without it the page is always replay.
- Light theme and palette from the existing `site/index.html`, so the two pages read as one product.
- `prefers-reduced-motion`: dots step instead of glide, no ambient sweep.

## 8. Scope against the deadline

The submission window opens Oct 12 at 19:00 IST, and the recording is at 15:00.

| Phase | What | Who | Time | Fits before recording? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Replay landing page** | Exporter for the Oct 11 run, replay JSON, frontend sections 1 to 8 in replay mode | Exporter: me, about 1.5 h. Frontend: your friend | Frontend is the long pole | Only if your friend has a solid day |
| **B. Live mode** | Three event sinks, observer service, live badge, Launch swarm button | Sinks and observer: me, about 3 h with tests. Frontend: live feed adapter, small | Tight. Touches the processes the live take depends on | Risky. Only after a full rehearsal |
| **C. AgentDojo swarm** | Section 6 visual from existing per-trace predictions | Frontend only, data already exists | Small | Yes, if A is on track |

My recommendation:
- **Ship A and C for the submission.** The public link shows a real recorded case end to end and both benchmarks, with no risk to the live take.
- **Record the demo video the planned way** (terminals, neatlogs, reports) and export that take as the second replay the same evening.
- **Build B after the hackathon** unless the rehearsal tonight goes clean and the frontend is done early. Adding hooks to all three processes the morning of the recording is the kind of change that breaks a live take.

## 9. Decisions (11 Oct)

1. Phase A and C for the submission. Phase B (live mode) after the hackathon.
2. The frontend is built from this file plus `site/replay/` and `site/data/` (see `site/replay/README.md`). Both data files exist now.
3. Hosting: GitHub Pages from `site/`.
4. The demo video is recorded the planned way (terminals, neatlogs, reports). That take gets exported as a second replay the same evening with `uv run python -m bench.replay <run_id> --watchdog-db runs/watchdog-oct12.duckdb`.

# Built-in browser

The built-in browser is a real browser pane inside the Claude desktop app, separate from the person's Chrome. Its tools are named `mcp__Claude_Browser__*` when the session itself runs inside the desktop app, and `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` when the session runs in the cloud (started from the web, a phone, or the desktop app) and is linked to the person's computer. The names after the prefix are the same either way, Claude uses whichever prefix is actually present, and this skill refers to the tools by the part after the prefix.

If the only built-in browser tool present is `enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser`, Claude calls it first: it turns the built-in browser on for this conversation, and the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` tools appear once it has run.

## What the person can see

The browser pane shares the desktop app's side panel with artifacts, documents, and file previews, and the panel shows one of them at a time. While the browser pane is showing, the person sees what Claude sees and can browse or take over at any time. While something else is open in the panel, or the panel is closed, the built-in browser keeps working but the person cannot see it.

Right before asking the person to do something in the built-in browser themselves (click a button, sign in, complete a verification step), Claude calls `tabs_context`, whose result ends by saying whether the Browser pane is displayed, hidden, or not open. If the pane is not open, Claude opens the page first and checks again. If the pane is hidden, Claude first asks the person to bring the browser back in the Claude desktop app: press Cmd+Shift+B on Mac or Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows, or close whatever else is open in the side panel and click the globe icon (the Browser button). Claude then says what to do in the browser. Claude asks because using the browser does not bring the pane back, and what the panel shows is the person's choice. Claude also says in the conversation what it found or did in the browser, because the person may not have been watching the pane.

## Sign-ins persist, and they are the person's

The built-in browser keeps its own persistent profile, shared across the desktop app's sessions. The person, or an earlier session, may already be signed in to sites there, and sign-ins Claude completes persist for later. Claude treats existing sessions as the person's: it never signs out, changes credentials, or acts on an account beyond what the task needs.

## Tabs

The built-in browser has tabs. `preview_start` with a `url` opens an additional tab at that URL in one call and returns a `tabId`, leaving existing tabs untouched, so Claude prefers it over `tabs_create` followed by `navigate` when the destination is already known. `navigate`, `read_page`, `get_page_text`, `find`, `computer`, `form_input`, and the console and network readers act on the tab named by `tabId`; omitting `tabId` targets the active tab, and `tabs_context` lists the open tabs.

## Loading via ToolSearch

Claude loads the built-in browser tools in bulk, not one-by-one: if they are in the deferred list, Claude loads them all in a single ToolSearch call whose query is their full name prefix, for example `{ query: "mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__", max_results: 64 }`.

## Reading pages

Claude prefers `get_page_text` and `read_page` over screenshots for reading, because they return the page's actual text and structure rather than pixels of the visible viewport. `computer` with action "screenshot" is for when the visual layout is the point or the person asks to see the page.

## Site approvals, blocked sites, and request_access

Depending on the person's approval settings, the person may be asked to approve a site before Claude acts on it, and some sites are blocked outright. Claude waits for a pending approval rather than working around it. If a page is refused or an approval is declined, Claude tells the person and moves on rather than retrying.

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, approvals can be answered from any of the person's devices and may take a moment to arrive, and the session may also have a `request_access` tool. If a browser tool answers that the site is not allowed yet and `request_access` is present, Claude calls it with that site's URL and scope "once" (or "site" when the task will keep using that site), waits for the person's answer, and then retries the original tool. Without `request_access`, a refused site is handled as above: Claude tells the person and moves on.

## What the built-in browser cannot open

The built-in browser cannot open `file://` URLs or `localhost` servers that Claude starts itself, because those run where Claude's shell runs, which is not where the browser pane runs. To show the person HTML that Claude generated, Claude uses an artifact instead.

## When the built-in browser cannot be reached

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, the pane runs in the Claude desktop app on the person's computer while Claude runs elsewhere, so it is reachable only while that app is open and online. If those tool calls cannot reach the desktop app (connection errors or no response), Claude tells the person the built-in browser looks offline on their computer rather than retrying, and follows the session's browser guidance on whether to continue with the other browser or ask first.

THE PROBLEM

A 25-year-old wiki became a notepad for thousands of agents.

DSEWiki has served German software developers for 25 years. In the summer of 2026, OpenAI agents writing under more than 3,700 self-given names used it as a shared notepad. They left an estimated 18,000 posts. Researchers later recovered 14,591 revisions.

content.text:
I went through Suprith's two "updated frontend" commits in a scratch worktree, so your checkout is untouched (you're still 2 behind origin). `npm ci`, the 5 vitest tests, `tsc` and `vite build` all pass. The committed `site/` is the same as a fresh build apart from line endings. I served it locally and it loads with no console errors. The numbers on it check out against the result files.

## What's wrong

**1. Running the build breaks the site.** `vite.config.ts` writes to `../site` and empties that folder first. But `frontend/public/` only holds the replay file, so a fresh `npm run build` deletes `site/data/exam.json`, `dojo.json`, `benchmarks.json`, `site/replay/README.md` and `efd78263e6d2.full.json`. The page then fails to load because it fetches `data/exam.json`. I reproduced this. The committed `site/` only works because those files got put back by hand. Fix: commit the data files under `frontend/public/` so the build copies them over.

**2. Junk got committed:** `.DS_Store`, `frontend/.vite/deps/` (Vite's cache, about 24k lines), and an empty root `package-lock.json`. I'd delete them and add `.DS_Store` and `.vite/` to `.gitignore`.

**3. The replay leaves out the agents breaking the rule.** His script builds the replay from the incident files only: 58 events, all `case.*`, starting at 07:26 when the first case opens. Your `bench.replay` export (now renamed `.full.json`) has all of it: 134 `agent.call` events with the `planted` flag, plus 25 `agent.blocked` events from the confirmation re-runs, starting at 07:08. His reducer already handles `agent.call` and `agent.blocked`. Right now the dots never go to Docs, never turn red, and never hit the guardrail barrier. The page's own note says re-run blocks "are not in this file", but they're in the export. That makes the core visual weaker than it needs to be.

**4. Live mode only exists on the frontend.** `?live=` makes the page call `/api/snapshot`, `/api/events` (a live event stream) and `POST /api/fleet`. Nothing in the backend serves those. The observer and event hooks (Phase B) were never built.

**5. GitHub Pages isn't set up.** There's no `.github/workflows` and the Pages API returns 404. Pages can't serve from a `site/` folder directly, so it needs an Actions workflow.

**6. Small mismatch.** The site says "Claude false alarms 104→26". The README says v0 "flagged 111" and the pipeline 29. Both are right: 111/29 count every flag, 104/26 count only the false ones on the security label. The voiceover just needs to match whichever number is on screen.

## Questions

1. **What does "wire it up for the demo" mean to you?**
   - **(a)** A replay site on Pages. This was the Oct 11 decision. It's safe and takes about an hour.
   - **(b)** Live mode tomorrow: event hooks in the arena, agents and watchdog, plus an observer service. That's about 3 hours with tests, and it touches every process the 15:00 live take depends on. I still think that's the wrong risk the night before recording. If you want it anyway, I'll do it after a full clean rehearsal, behind a flag, with the hooks writing in the background so they can't stall the pipeline.
2. **Point the player at the full export (agent calls and guardrail blocks)?** I'd add those events into his cut rather than swap files, so his `label`, `agents`, `note` and `cited` fields stay. One catch: the re-runs add 13 runs' worth of agents, so I'd show re-run agents as short-lived dots, as the proposal describes.
3. **Is it fine for me to commit cleanups on top of Suprith's work?** Or will he push more tonight? If he's still working, I'd rather send him the list than end up with merge conflicts.

## What I'll do once you answer (assuming 1a, yes to 2)

1. Fast-forward local main to origin.
2. Remove the junk and fix `.gitignore`.
3. Move `exam.json`, `dojo.json`, `benchmarks.json` and the full export into `frontend/public/`. Change `build_public_data.py` to add in the agent calls and blocks.
4. Add a test that fails if a build is missing the data files.
5. Rebuild `site/` and check every section in the browser.
6. Add a Pages workflow that deploys `site/`. Enabling Pages in the repo settings is a change on GitHub, so I'll ask before I flip it.
7. Update the cheat sheet so the numbers on screen match the voiceover.

content.thinking:
I'm thinking through where the full export JSON should actually live, since the build process wipes the site directory—it needs to source from frontend/public/replay rather than site/replay so it survives rebuilds.

For the merge logic, I'll pull run.started, agent.call, agent.blocked, and case.remembered from the full export, but deliberately skip case.failed since the reducer would render it awkwardly with mismatched fields and the cut never included it originally—not worth the risk. I also note the full export's case.confirming includes rerun_ids that the cut currently leaves empty, with a note explaining guardrail block spans instead.

I'm filling in those rerun_ids and updating the note accordingly, and planning the reducer identity logic for re-run agents: keying agents by `${agent}@${run_id}` for confirm/control kinds, tracking a run mode and ghost flag per AgentState via a helper function. Now I'm working out where ghost agents render visually—likely in the region near the Notes board—and how they bounce off the barrier at the notes node using positional offsets.

The current y-offset formula breaks down for ghost indices above a few dozen, so I need dedicated ghost home positions in a grid in the lower half of the field, distinct from live agent homes and other fixed nodes, with small unlabeled dots in a lighter tone. The trickier issue is visibility duration—since there's no explicit "finished" event in the export, I'm considering having each ghost fade out some fixed virtual duration after its last recorded event rather than relying on a true completion signal.

Thinking through the compressed-time replay, I decide a ghost should stay visible if less than roughly 12 seconds has passed since its spawn or last call, whichever is more recent—gaps within a run are short enough that this keeps it showing throughout, while gaps between runs let it fade. I'm also now working out how to lay out the potentially 36 concurrent ghosts from three parallel runs of 12 agents each, trying rows of them in the lower band of the field while avoiding collisions with the Submit and Unlisted nodes.

I settle on a better placement idea: cluster each run's ghosts in a small orbit around their parent agent's now-empty home position, since the real agent gets moved to a confirmation cage elsewhere. This reads naturally as "new copies of this agent running" and keeps the layout organized by parent rather than scattered. I plan to route each ghost's travel from its own home to the service along the same path logic as the live agents, with slight positional offsets near notes to avoid overlap, and I start sketching the home-position lookup logic that checks whether an agent has a parent.

For block and trail behavior, I decide ghosts should only flash a brief red bounce when they hit a forbidden path rather than persisting a red trail, keeping the forbidden-write logic otherwise honest in case a rerun actually succeeds in writing. I also note that control-run ghosts should cluster the same way, keeping things simple rather than giving them a distinct visual treatment, and move on to thinking through hit-testing.

Hit-testing needs to work for ghosts too, so I'm refining how agent labels display — using a format combining agent id, run kind, and a short run_id slice so re-run events read clearly in both AgentEvidence and EventStack, since currently EventStack's label pulls raw agent names in a way that could misleadingly suggest the original agent rather than the re-run.

For the hero, the first minute of activity (07:08:23–07:09:29) stays accurate for the footer text. I'm leaning toward removing agent.blocked from STATE_TYPES since 25 individual block hops would make "Next state" navigation clunky during playback — better UX to drop it even though it's a minor design call. The "0/3 fixed" counter logic using state.order.length as fallback looks fine as is.

Thinking through the build/deploy setup more, I'm debating whether to let CI build site/ from source via npm each time versus keeping the committed site/ as the deploy artifact — leaning toward having the workflow run npm ci, npm test, and npm run build to avoid drift between src and the built output, while still keeping site/ committed since docs reference it directly.

Writing reducer logic...

Now I'm figuring out visibility: reruns should only draw when virtual time has passed their spawn point and they haven't gone stale, using a linger window (~12s) after their last activity before they disappear, since I need to account for LLM latency gaps and the compressed-time scrubbing behavior. I also need to make sure hit-testing and evidence lookups skip invisible rerun agents, so I'm adding a visibility check to filter them out.

For positioning, I'm storing a parentIndex directly on each agent's state instead of looking up the parent each time, then arranging rerun children in an orbit around their parent's home position—spacing up to twelve slots per parent at varying radii, calibrated against the normalized home coordinates and the field's pixel dimensions.

Since the live parent dot gets caged off to the side during confirmation, its home slot sits empty while the ghost children surround it, which works well visually. I'm generalizing the travel calculation to pull each agent's home via a homeOf function, adding a slight vertical jitter when ghosts bounce off blocked states, and rendering ghosts as smaller rings with a translucent dark fill (no label, minimal halo) that fade in and out, while keeping the red trail logic restricted to non-ghost agents unless explicitly marked red.

Now I'm going through consumers of the state model to make sure everything still works with ghosts added: removing the "agent.blocked" state type since it's no longer needed, swapping agentLabel for agentKey in the event stack, confirming wobble animation still indexes correctly for ghost slots, checking that hitAgent properly skips invisible agents during hit-testing, and verifying that AgentEvidence labels render sensibly for ghost entries like "research_agent_1 · confirm" variants. # Site data

Everything the frontend needs, as static JSON. Architecture and the event schema are in `docs/frontend/proposal.md`.

## `replay/efd78263e6d2.full.json`: the Oct 11 live run, flag to fixed

This is the `bench.replay` export. The landing page plays a shorter cut, `replay/efd78263e6d2.json`, built by `frontend/scripts/build_public_data.py` (58 events, player fields `label`, `agents`, `note`). Regenerating the export overwrites `efd78263e6d2.json`; move that output back to `efd78263e6d2.full.json` and rebuild the cut before shipping.

- `runs`: every run in the replay and its role: `live` (the three agents), `confirm` (re-runs after a patch), `control` (a clean scenario run alongside).
- `cases`: one summary per case: agent, final status, detected by, neatlogs trace link, findings with the verifier's verdict, patch commit and Entire checkpoint, confirmation result.
- `events`: 234 events sorted by time, each `{seq, ts, source, type, run_id, agent, case_id, data}`.

| type | count | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `run.started` | 13 | a run began: 1 live, 9 confirm re-runs, 3 controls |
| `agent.call` | 134 | an agent's tool call: service (`docs`, `data`, `notes`), path, and `planted` when the page it read carried the planted note |
| `agent.blocked` | 25 | a patched guardrail stopped a re-run's call to the notes board |
| `case.opened` | 3 | the watchdog opened a case; `detected_by` is native, local or both |
| `case.transition` | 27 | a state change, `from` and `to` |
| `case.findings` | 3 | the investigator's findings |
| `case.verdict` | 3 | the same findings after the verifier, with `verdict` and `reason` |
| `case.writeback` | 13 | tags written to neatlogs, and span feedback attempts (`ok` false on Oct 11: CLI login had expired) |
| `case.patched` | 3 | patch commit sha, Entire checkpoint, files |
| `case.confirming` | 3 | the re-run and control run ids |
| `case.confirmed` | 3 | re-runs clean, control clean, watchdog view clean |
| `case.failed` | 1 | case 37fa7776: the investigator hit a neatlogs rate limit, the fallback model finished the job |
| `case.remembered` | 3 | the incident was stored in Entire Brain |

Timing to know for the player: agents run 12:38:23 to 12:39:29 IST, cases open at 12:56:22 (the watchdog was being restarted during this run), patches land within about a minute, confirmation takes 6 to 10 minutes. Compress the gaps.

## `data/benchmarks.json`

- `held_out`: our 102-trace exam. Aggregate counts and rates for `v0` and `final` (Bladerunner). Per-trace predictions were not saved for this run, so draw any grid from the counts.
- `agentdojo`: 858 published runs. `summary` per checker and label, and `runs` with one entry per run: `model`, `suite`, `attacked`, `acted` (made the attacker's call), `security` (AgentDojo's strict label), and whether `v0` and `bladerunner` flagged it.

## Regenerate

```bash
uv run python -m bench.replay efd78263e6d2
mv site/replay/efd78263e6d2.json site/replay/efd78263e6d2.full.json
```

```bash
uv run python -m bench.site_data
```

-# Bladerunner frontend: landing page and live mission control
-Proposal for one site that tells the story and shows the system working. Architecture, flow, data contract and scope. No implementation here.
-1. **Landing page.** Anyone opening the link understands the problem, sees Bladerunner catch an agent, and sees the numbers.

-2. **Mission control.** The same page, pointed at a running Bladerunner on this laptop, shows the swarm of agents working, the moment one breaks a rule, and every step of the case until it is fixed, live.
-Both jobs use the same screen and the same components. The only difference is where the events come from.
-| Mode | Where events come from | Who sees it | Needs a backend |
-| **Replay** | A recorded event file shipped with the site (the Oct 11 run, tomorrow's live take, AgentDojo results) | Everyone, on the public link | No. Static hosting (GitHub Pages, Vercel) |
-| **Live** | A local observer service streaming events while the arena, fleet and watchdog run | Us, during the demo recording | Yes, on 127.0.0.1 only |
-A badge in the corner always says which mode is on: `LIVE` or `REPLAY · 11 Oct 2026, run efd78263e6d2`. Replay never pretends to be live.
-| # | Section | What the viewer sees | Data |

-| 1 | **Hero: the swarm** | Full-width canvas. Agents as small bright dots drifting between service nodes (Data API, Docs, Notes board). A thin scanning line sweeps the field: the watchdog reading traces. One headline, one sentence, two buttons: "Watch a case" and "See the numbers". | Replay event stream, looping the first 60 seconds of the Oct 11 run |
-| 2 | **The problem** | The DSEWiki story, short. The existing `site/index.html` narration can be reused here. | Static copy |

-| 3 | **Watch a case** (the core) | Mission control, full screen height. Swarm on the left, case pipeline on the right, evidence drawer below. Plays one case from flag to fixed in about 60 seconds of compressed time, with a scrubber. | Replay stream for one case, or Live stream |

-| 4 | **How it decides** | Three short panels: rules catch it, an investigator explains it, a verifier from another model family checks it. Each panel lights up the matching pipeline step in section 3 when scrolled to. | Static copy plus the real finding text from the case |

-| 5 | **Test 1: our exam** | The 102-trace result. Two columns of 102 small squares, v0 and Bladerunner, colored by right alarm, false alarm, miss, correct silence. | `bench/results/v0.json`, `final.json` |

-| 6 | **Test 2: other people's agents** | The AgentDojo swarm: 858 dots in three clusters (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.3 70B). Toggle v0 vs Bladerunner and watch the false-alarm dots on the Claude cluster drop from 111 to 29. | `bench/external/agentdojo/results/*.json` (per-trace predictions are already in there) |
-| 7 | **Built with** | neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai, one line each plus one real artifact each: a trace link, an `entire why` line, the plan headline numbers. | Static copy |
-This is the "show the working" piece. It is one component used by the hero (cropped, ambient) and section 3 (full).
-- **Swarm field** (left, about 60% width). Service nodes are fixed: Data API `:8101`, Docs `:8103`, Notes board `:8102`, Unlisted `:8104`, Submit. Agents are particles.

-- **Case pipeline** (right). One card per open case. Each card is a vertical stepper of the real states: flagged, paused, investigating, investigated, verified, quarantined, patching, patched, confirming, fixed. Failure endings get their own color: needs_review, not_fixed, dismissed.

-- **Evidence drawer** (bottom, collapsed until a step is clicked). Shows the real artifact for that step: the offending span input, the investigator's claim, the verifier's verdict, the guardrail diff, the `entire why` line, the confirmation result.
-- **Timeline scrubber** (bottom edge). Real timestamps. Long waits (finalization, confirmation re-runs) are compressed and marked as "6 min skipped".
-Every animation maps to one real event. Nothing moves without an event behind it.
-| Agent makes a tool call | The agent's dot travels to that service node and back |
-| The call reads planted content | The Docs node pulses amber for that agent only |
-| The call goes somewhere the policy forbids | The dot's trail turns red and stays red |
-| Trace lands in neatlogs | A faint ring around the agent's dot |
-| Case opened | A card slides into the pipeline, linked to the agent by a thin line |
-| Paused | The agent's dot freezes in place |
-| Investigation and verification | The card's stepper advances; the drawer offers the claim and verdict text |
-| Quarantined | The dot is pulled into a dashed cage at the edge of the field |
-| Patched | A barrier line is drawn around the Notes board node, labeled with the commit sha |
-| Confirmation re-runs | New dots for the re-run agents; when one tries the forbidden call it bounces off the barrier (a guardrail block) |
-| Fixed | The card turns green, the caged dot is released grey, the barrier stays |
-| Brain remembers | A small "remembered" chip on the card |
-- Click an agent: its tool-call list in the drawer, and a link to its trace in neatlogs.
-- Click a case card: its incident report fields in the drawer.
-- Scrubber: pause, play, 1x, 10x, jump to next state change.
-- Live mode only: a **Launch swarm** button with an agent count (3, 6, 12) and scenario (`planted_dev`, `clean_dev`). It starts a fleet run through the observer.
-### Making it feel like a swarm
-Three real agents look thin on a hero. Options, all honest:
-- **Live:** `fleet.cli run --agents N` already takes any N. Twelve agents on `planted_dev` is a real swarm of real agents. Cost is about 4x the 3-agent run and more neatlogs load.
-- **Replay hero:** the Oct 11 run plus the re-runs and controls it spawned (3 agents, 9 re-runs, 3 control runs) is 15 real agents across one case cycle.
-- **Section 6:** the 858 AgentDojo runs are the big swarm, clearly labeled as recorded runs from another lab's benchmark.
-1. **Frontend** (static site). Renders the page. Talks to one interface, `EventFeed`, and never knows whether it is live or replay.
-2. **Replay files** (static JSON, shipped with the site). One file per recorded run, in the event schema below, plus the two benchmark result sets.

-3. **Replay exporter** (Python script, offline). Builds a replay file from what a finished run left behind: `watchdog.duckdb` case events, `truth.duckdb` agent requests, `runs/incidents/*.json`, git commits, and the re-run traces from neatlogs for guardrail blocks.
-4. **Event sinks** (small hooks inside existing processes, live mode only). Each process appends events to its own JSON-lines file under `runs/live/`.
-5. **Observer** (small local web service, live mode only). Tails `runs/live/`, merges and streams events to the browser, serves a few read endpoints, and can start a fleet run.
-### Why files and an observer, instead of reading the databases

-DuckDB lets one process hold a database for writing. While the watchdog runs it holds `watchdog.duckdb`, and the arena holds `truth.duckdb`, so a separate viewer cannot read either live. Appending one line per event to a file is the smallest change that lets a viewer follow along without touching the databases or the pipeline's timing.
-| Arena | `ArenaState.log_request` (every agent request, with `planted`) and run registration in control | `runs/live/arena.jsonl` |

-| Each agent process | `ToolExecutor._blocked` in `arena/tools.py` (guardrail blocks never reach the arena request log today) and the run start and stop | `runs/live/agent-<run>-<agent>.jsonl`, one writer per file |
